claim: Intraperitoneal injections of CNO at doses of 1, 5, and 10 mg/kg alter sleep in wild-type male laboratory mice.
source: Here, we show that intraperitoneal injections of commonly used CNO doses (1, 5, and 10 mg/kg) alter sleep in wild-type male laboratory mice.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data from EEG/EMG recordings showing changes in sleep parameters following CNO injections.

claim: CNO causes dose-dependent suppression of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep.
source: Using electroencephalography (EEG) and electromyography (EMG) to analyse sleep, we found a dose-dependent suppression of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, changes in EEG spectral power during non-REM (NREM) sleep, and altered sleep architecture in a pattern previously reported for clozapine.
evidence: The manuscript presents dose-response data showing REM sleep suppression at different CNO doses.

claim: CNO causes changes in EEG spectral power during NREM sleep.
source: Using electroencephalography (EEG) and electromyography (EMG) to analyse sleep, we found a dose-dependent suppression of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, changes in EEG spectral power during non-REM (NREM) sleep, and altered sleep architecture in a pattern previously reported for clozapine.
evidence: The manuscript presents spectral analysis data showing changes in EEG power during NREM sleep.

claim: CNO alters sleep architecture in a pattern previously reported for clozapine.
source: Using electroencephalography (EEG) and electromyography (EMG) to analyse sleep, we found a dose-dependent suppression of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, changes in EEG spectral power during non-REM (NREM) sleep, and altered sleep architecture in a pattern previously reported for clozapine.
evidence: The manuscript presents sleep architecture data and compares the pattern to previously published clozapine effects.

claim: Effects of CNO on sleep could arise from back-metabolism to clozapine.
source: Effects of CNO on sleep could arise from back-metabolism to clozapine or binding to endogenous neurotransmitter receptors.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms underlying the observed effects.

claim: Effects of CNO on sleep could arise from binding to endogenous neurotransmitter receptors.
source: Effects of CNO on sleep could arise from back-metabolism to clozapine or binding to endogenous neurotransmitter receptors.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms underlying the observed effects.

claim: Compound 21 (C21, 3 mg/kg) modulates sleep despite a lack of back-metabolism to clozapine.
source: Interestingly, we found that the novel DREADD actuator, compound 21 (C21, 3 mg/kg), similarly modulates sleep despite a lack of back-metabolism to clozapine.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing sleep modulation by C21 and cites literature showing C21 does not convert to clozapine.

claim: Both CNO and C21 can modulate sleep of mice not expressing DREADD receptors.
source: Our results demonstrate that both CNO and C21 can modulate sleep of mice not expressing DREADD receptors.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data from wild-type mice showing sleep modulation by both compounds.

claim: Back-metabolism to clozapine is not the sole mechanism underlying side effects of chemogenetic actuators.
source: This implies that back-metabolism to clozapine is not the sole mechanism underlying side effects of chemogenetic actuators.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that C21, which does not convert to clozapine, still modulates sleep.

claim: Any chemogenetic experiment should include a DREADD-free control group injected with the same CNO, C21, or newly developed actuator.
source: Therefore, any chemogenetic experiment should include a DREADD-free control group injected with the same CNO, C21, or newly developed actuator.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings that actuators can have effects independent of DREADD activation.

claim: Electrophysiological sleep assessment could serve as a sensitive tool to test the biological inertness of novel chemogenetic actuators.
source: We suggest that electrophysiological sleep assessment could serve as a sensitive tool to test the biological inertness of novel chemogenetic actuators.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the sensitivity of sleep measures to detect effects of CNO and C21.

claim: DREADDs enable non-invasive and cell type-specific remote control of neuronal activity in freely moving animals on a time scale of minutes to hours.
source: Designer receptors exclusively activated by designer drugs (DREADDs) enable non-invasive and cell type-specific remote control of neuronal activity in freely moving animals on a time scale of minutes to hours (Roth, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work describing DREADD technology.

claim: DREADD technology is a powerful tool to probe the contribution of selected neuronal populations in controlling vigilance states.
source: In the context of sleep research, these characteristics make DREADD technology a powerful tool with which to probe the contribution of selected neuronal populations in controlling vigilance states (Hayashi et al., 2015; Varin et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2019; Mondino et al., 2021), sleep state-specific network oscillations (Funk et al., 2017; Vaidyanathan et al., 2021), as well as sleep-related physiology (Harding et al., 2018; Fleury Curado et al., 2018) and behaviour (Eban-Rothschild et al., 2016; Tossell et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies using DREADDs in sleep research.

claim: Early work suggested that CNO is pharmacologically inert.
source: Early work suggested that CNO is pharmacologically inert (Armbruster et al., 2007) and not back-metabolised to its parent drug clozapine in mice (Guettier et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to early studies on CNO.

claim: Early work suggested that CNO is not back-metabolised to clozapine in mice.
source: Early work suggested that CNO is pharmacologically inert (Armbruster et al., 2007) and not back-metabolised to its parent drug clozapine in mice (Guettier et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an early study on CNO metabolism.

claim: More recent studies demonstrated relevant conversion of CNO to pharmacologically active metabolites including clozapine.
source: However, more recent studies demonstrated relevant conversion of CNO to pharmacologically active metabolites including clozapine (Gomez et al., 2017; Manvich et al., 2018; Jendryka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies showing CNO metabolism.

claim: Clozapine is an atypical antipsychotic drug used in the treatment of schizophrenia with a high affinity for dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors.
source: Clozapine is an atypical antipsychotic drug used in the treatment of schizophrenia with a high affinity for dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors coupled with a broad binding profile to cholinergic, adrenergic, histaminergic, and serotonergic receptors (Wenthur and Lindsley, 2013), which may account for its high efficacy compared to other antipsychotics (Kane et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to pharmacological literature on clozapine.

claim: Clozapine has a broad binding profile to cholinergic, adrenergic, histaminergic, and serotonergic receptors.
source: Clozapine is an atypical antipsychotic drug used in the treatment of schizophrenia with a high affinity for dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors coupled with a broad binding profile to cholinergic, adrenergic, histaminergic, and serotonergic receptors (Wenthur and Lindsley, 2013), which may account for its high efficacy compared to other antipsychotics (Kane et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to pharmacological literature on clozapine.

claim: CNO presents off-target binding at a broad range of neurotransmitter receptors.
source: In addition, CNO itself was found to present off-target binding at a broad range of neurotransmitter receptors (Gomez et al., 2017; Jendryka et al., 2019) and to elicit behavioural effects (Gomez et al., 2017; Manvich et al., 2018; MacLaren et al., 2016) at doses commonly used for DREADD experiments.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies characterizing CNO's off-target binding.

claim: CNO elicits behavioural effects at doses commonly used for DREADD experiments.
source: In addition, CNO itself was found to present off-target binding at a broad range of neurotransmitter receptors (Gomez et al., 2017; Jendryka et al., 2019) and to elicit behavioural effects (Gomez et al., 2017; Manvich et al., 2018; MacLaren et al., 2016) at doses commonly used for DREADD experiments.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing behavioral effects of CNO.

claim: A comprehensive assessment of putative dose-dependent effects of CNO on sleep in wild-type mice has never been systematically conducted.
source: However, a comprehensive assessment of putative dose-dependent effects of CNO on sleep in wild-type mice has never been systematically conducted, although a recent study reported that high CNO doses affected sleep in DREADD-free control animals (Varin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in the literature, supported by noting that only one study reported effects.

claim: A recent study reported that high CNO doses affected sleep in DREADD-free control animals.
source: However, a comprehensive assessment of putative dose-dependent effects of CNO on sleep in wild-type mice has never been systematically conducted, although a recent study reported that high CNO doses affected sleep in DREADD-free control animals (Varin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study showing CNO effects on sleep.

claim: Clozapine is a sedating antipsychotic drug.
source: This is an important omission, given that clozapine is a sedating antipsychotic drug (Leucht et al., 2013) known to modulate sleep in humans (Hinze-Selch et al., 1997; Monti et al., 2017; Riemann and Nissen, 2012) and laboratory rodents (Spierings et al., 1977; Sorge et al., 2004; Grønli et al., 2016; Coward et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to clinical literature on clozapine.

claim: Clozapine modulates sleep in humans.
source: This is an important omission, given that clozapine is a sedating antipsychotic drug (Leucht et al., 2013) known to modulate sleep in humans (Hinze-Selch et al., 1997; Monti et al., 2017; Riemann and Nissen, 2012) and laboratory rodents (Spierings et al., 1977; Sorge et al., 2004; Grønli et al., 2016; Coward et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to human sleep studies with clozapine.

claim: Clozapine modulates sleep in laboratory rodents.
source: This is an important omission, given that clozapine is a sedating antipsychotic drug (Leucht et al., 2013) known to modulate sleep in humans (Hinze-Selch et al., 1997; Monti et al., 2017; Riemann and Nissen, 2012) and laboratory rodents (Spierings et al., 1977; Sorge et al., 2004; Grønli et al., 2016; Coward et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to rodent sleep studies with clozapine.

claim: Many endogenous neurotransmitter receptors that are drug targets of clozapine are involved in the regulation of arousal and sleep.
source: Many of the endogenous neurotransmitter receptors, which are drug targets of clozapine (Wenthur and Lindsley, 2013) and to which CNO presents off-target binding affinity (Jendryka et al., 2019; Gomez et al., 2017), are also involved in the regulation of arousal and sleep (Saper and Fuller, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on clozapine pharmacology, CNO off-target binding, and sleep neurobiology.

claim: C21 does not convert to clozapine.
source: Initially intended as a control experiment, we here tested whether commonly used doses of CNO (1, 5, and 10 mg/kg) and the novel DREADD agonist compound 21 (C21), which does not convert to clozapine (Thompson et al., 2018) but has an off-target binding profile similar to CNO (Jendryka et al., 2019), affect sleep in wild-type C57BL/6J mice under laboratory conditions.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a pharmacokinetic study of C21.

claim: C21 has an off-target binding profile similar to CNO.
source: Initially intended as a control experiment, we here tested whether commonly used doses of CNO (1, 5, and 10 mg/kg) and the novel DREADD agonist compound 21 (C21), which does not convert to clozapine (Thompson et al., 2018) but has an off-target binding profile similar to CNO (Jendryka et al., 2019), affect sleep in wild-type C57BL/6J mice under laboratory conditions.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study characterizing C21's binding profile.

claim: There was no significant main effect of CNO treatment on the proportion of time spent awake in the first 2 hours after injection.
source: There was no significant main effect of the treatment condition on the proportion of time spent awake, in NREM sleep or in REM sleep.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There was a non-significant trend towards a main effect of CNO treatment on NREM sleep proportion (F(1.911, 23.57)=3.054, p=0.0682).
source: However, there was a non-significant trend towards a main effect of the treatment condition for NREM sleep (F(1.911, 23.57)=3.054, p=0.0682, Figure 1b) and REM sleep (F(2.366, 29.18)=2.590, p=0.0839, Figure 1b) consistent with a report of a short-lasting increase of NREM sleep and decrease of REM sleep following CNO injections of 5 and 10 mg/kg (Varin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There was a non-significant trend towards a main effect of CNO treatment on REM sleep proportion (F(2.366, 29.18)=2.590, p=0.0839).
source: However, there was a non-significant trend towards a main effect of the treatment condition for NREM sleep (F(1.911, 23.57)=3.054, p=0.0682, Figure 1b) and REM sleep (F(2.366, 29.18)=2.590, p=0.0839, Figure 1b) consistent with a report of a short-lasting increase of NREM sleep and decrease of REM sleep following CNO injections of 5 and 10 mg/kg (Varin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: CNO treatment significantly affected the amount of REM sleep relative to total sleep time in the first 2 hours (F(1.783, 21.99)=8.951, p=0.0019).
source: As the entry to REM sleep requires the previous occurrence of NREM sleep, we also analysed REM sleep as proportion of total sleep time and found a significant effect of CNO treatment on the amount of REM sleep relative to the total sleep time (F(1.783, 21.99)=8.951, p=0.0019, Figure 1b), due to a significantly reduced REM/NREM sleep ratio following injections of high CNO doses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: CNO injections resulted in a significantly reduced REM/NREM sleep ratio following high doses.
source: As the entry to REM sleep requires the previous occurrence of NREM sleep, we also analysed REM sleep as proportion of total sleep time and found a significant effect of CNO treatment on the amount of REM sleep relative to the total sleep time (F(1.783, 21.99)=8.951, p=0.0019, Figure 1b), due to a significantly reduced REM/NREM sleep ratio following injections of high CNO doses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis shown in a figure.

claim: CNO concentrations in blood plasma, cerebrospinal fluid, and brain tissue of mice peak within the first 15–30 min after intraperitoneal and subcutaneous injections.
source: We initially focussed on an acute (first 2 hr) time window because CNO concentrations in blood plasma, cerebrospinal fluid, and brain tissue of mice peak within the first 15–30 min after both intraperitoneal and subcutaneous injections (Jendryka et al., 2019; Manvich et al., 2018), and behavioural side effects are typically tested within the first 2 hr following drug administration (MacLaren et al., 2016; Manvich et al., 2018; Gomez et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to pharmacokinetic studies of CNO.

claim: REM sleep as proportion of total sleep time was significantly altered over the 6 hour observation period (F(1.839,22.68)=7.525, p=0.0038).
source: Relative to the total sleep time, the proportion of REM sleep was significantly altered (F(1.839,22.68)=7.525, p=0.0038, Figure 1b) due to a reduced REM/NREM sleep ratio following medium and high doses of CNO (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: CNO injections elicited unusually long NREM bouts (main effect maximum NREM episode duration: F(2.881,35.53)=13.24, p<0.0001).
source: CNO injections elicited unusually long NREM bouts (main effect maximum NREM episode duration: F(2.881,35.53)=13.24, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There were longer NREM sleep episodes on average following CNO injections (main effect mean NREM episode duration: F(2.436,30.04)=11.64, p<0.0001).
source: On average, there were longer (main effect mean NREM episode duration: F(2.436,30.04)=11.64, p<0.0001) but fewer (main effect NREM episode number: F (2.476,30.54)=7.796, p=0.0010) NREM sleep episodes following CNO injections.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There were fewer NREM sleep episodes following CNO injections (main effect NREM episode number: F(2.476,30.54)=7.796, p=0.0010).
source: On average, there were longer (main effect mean NREM episode duration: F(2.436,30.04)=11.64, p<0.0001) but fewer (main effect NREM episode number: F (2.476,30.54)=7.796, p=0.0010) NREM sleep episodes following CNO injections.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The latency between injection and onset of NREM sleep was significantly affected by CNO injections (F(2.146,26.47)=3.380, p=0.0463).
source: The latency between the injection and the onset of NREM sleep was also significantly affected by CNO injections (F(2.146,26.47)=3.380, p=0.0463, Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There was a significant main effect of CNO treatment on the mean REM episode duration (F(2.150,26.52)=4.230, p=0.0232).
source: While the maximum duration of REM sleep episodes was not altered by CNO, there was a significant main effect of the treatment on the mean REM episode duration (F(2.150,26.52)=4.230, p=0.0232) and number of REM episodes (F(2.124,26.19)=6.430, p=0.0047).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There was a significant main effect of CNO treatment on the number of REM episodes (F(2.124,26.19)=6.430, p=0.0047).
source: While the maximum duration of REM sleep episodes was not altered by CNO, there was a significant main effect of the treatment on the mean REM episode duration (F(2.150,26.52)=4.230, p=0.0232) and number of REM episodes (F(2.124,26.19)=6.430, p=0.0047).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The latency between sleep onset and the first transition to REM sleep was significantly changed by CNO (F(1.840,22.69)=4.691, p=0.0220).
source: Also, the latency between sleep onset and the first transition to REM sleep was significantly changed (F(1.840,22.69)=4.691, p=0.0220) with a significantly delayed REM onset in the 1 and 10 mg/kg conditions (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: CNO injections were followed by a small but significant increase in spectral power in the range between 0.5 and 1.25 Hz during NREM sleep over the first 2 hours.
source: We observed that CNO injections were followed by a small but significant increase in spectral power in the range between 0.5 and 1.25 Hz and suppression of spectral power in nearly all frequency bins between 6 and 30 Hz during NREM sleep over the first 2 hr (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from spectral analysis of EEG data.

claim: CNO injections were followed by suppression of spectral power in nearly all frequency bins between 6 and 30 Hz during NREM sleep over the first 2 hours.
source: We observed that CNO injections were followed by a small but significant increase in spectral power in the range between 0.5 and 1.25 Hz and suppression of spectral power in nearly all frequency bins between 6 and 30 Hz during NREM sleep over the first 2 hr (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from spectral analysis of EEG data.

claim: The suppression of power above 6 Hz during NREM sleep was robust and remained significant for both the acute (2 hr) and the prolonged (6 hr) observation period.
source: While the increase in slow frequency bins during NREM sleep appeared to be temporary and did not persist after Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple testing (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995), the systematic suppression of power above 6 Hz was more robust and remained significant for both the acute (2 hr) and the prolonged (6 hr) observation period (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from spectral analysis of EEG data with statistical correction.

claim: There were significant main effects of CNO treatment on NREM sleep before REM onset (F(2.031,25.04)=5.087, p=0.0137).
source: For the sleep stability measures there were significant main effects of the treatment condition (NREM before REM: F(2.031,25.04)=5.087, p=0.0137; brief awakenings: F(1.968,23.6)=10.38, p=0.0006).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There were significant main effects of CNO treatment on brief awakenings (F(1.968,23.6)=10.38, p=0.0006).
source: For the sleep stability measures there were significant main effects of the treatment condition (NREM before REM: F(2.031,25.04)=5.087, p=0.0137; brief awakenings: F(1.968,23.6)=10.38, p=0.0006).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The percentage of REM sleep was significantly reduced over the 6 hr observation period following C21 injection both in relation to the total sleep time (t(6) = 3.234, p=0.0089, Cohen's d=–1.2223).
source: The percentage of REM sleep was significantly reduced over the 6 hr observation period both in relation to the total sleep time (t(6) = 3.234, p=0.0089, Cohen's d=–1.2223, Figure 4) and to the recording time (t(6) = 2.086, p=0.0410, Cohen's d=–0.7885) with a strongly reduced REM to NREM ratio (t(6) = 3.253, p=0.0087, Cohen's d=–1.2296, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis of C21 effects.

claim: The percentage of REM sleep was significantly reduced over the 6 hr observation period following C21 injection in relation to the recording time (t(6) = 2.086, p=0.0410, Cohen's d=–0.7885).
source: The percentage of REM sleep was significantly reduced over the 6 hr observation period both in relation to the total sleep time (t(6) = 3.234, p=0.0089, Cohen's d=–1.2223, Figure 4) and to the recording time (t(6) = 2.086, p=0.0410, Cohen's d=–0.7885) with a strongly reduced REM to NREM ratio (t(6) = 3.253, p=0.0087, Cohen's d=–1.2296, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis of C21 effects.

claim: C21 injection resulted in a strongly reduced REM to NREM ratio (t(6) = 3.253, p=0.0087, Cohen's d=–1.2296).
source: The percentage of REM sleep was significantly reduced over the 6 hr observation period both in relation to the total sleep time (t(6) = 3.234, p=0.0089, Cohen's d=–1.2223, Figure 4) and to the recording time (t(6) = 2.086, p=0.0410, Cohen's d=–0.7885) with a strongly reduced REM to NREM ratio (t(6) = 3.253, p=0.0087, Cohen's d=–1.2296, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis of C21 effects.

claim: C21 increased the maximum duration of NREM sleep episodes (t(6) = 2.551, p=0.0217, Cohen's d=0.9641).
source: The maximum and average duration of NREM sleep episodes was increased (maximum duration: t(6) = 2.551, p=0.0217, Cohen's d=0.9641; mean duration: t(6) = 2.462, p=0.0245, Cohen's d=0.9307) while the number of NREM sleep episodes in the first 6 hr following C21 injection was reduced (t(6) = 2.809, p=0.0154, Cohen's d=–1.0617; Figure 5a, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis of C21 effects.

claim: C21 increased the average duration of NREM sleep episodes (t(6) = 2.462, p=0.0245, Cohen's d=0.9307).
source: The maximum and average duration of NREM sleep episodes was increased (maximum duration: t(6) = 2.551, p=0.0217, Cohen's d=0.9641; mean duration: t(6) = 2.462, p=0.0245, Cohen's d=0.9307) while the number of NREM sleep episodes in the first 6 hr following C21 injection was reduced (t(6) = 2.809, p=0.0154, Cohen's d=–1.0617; Figure 5a, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis of C21 effects.

claim: C21 reduced the number of NREM sleep episodes (t(6) = 2.809, p=0.0154, Cohen's d=–1.0617).
source: The maximum and average duration of NREM sleep episodes was increased (maximum duration: t(6) = 2.551, p=0.0217, Cohen's d=0.9641; mean duration: t(6) = 2.462, p=0.0245, Cohen's d=0.9307) while the number of NREM sleep episodes in the first 6 hr following C21 injection was reduced (t(6) = 2.809, p=0.0154, Cohen's d=–1.0617; Figure 5a, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis of C21 effects.

claim: C21 increased the mean REM episode duration (t(6) = 2.082, p=0.0413, Cohen's d=0.7869).
source: For REM episodes there was no C21 effect on the maximum duration, however the mean REM episode duration was increased (t(6) = 2.082, p=0.0413, Cohen's d=0.7869), the number of REM episodes reduced (t(6) = 4.942, p=0.0013, Cohen's d=–1.8679) and the onset of REM sleep was delayed (t(6) = 2.043, p=0.0435, Cohen's d=0.7722, Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis of C21 effects.

claim: C21 reduced the number of REM episodes (t(6) = 4.942, p=0.0013, Cohen's d=–1.8679).
source: For REM episodes there was no C21 effect on the maximum duration, however the mean REM episode duration was increased (t(6) = 2.082, p=0.0413, Cohen's d=0.7869), the number of REM episodes reduced (t(6) = 4.942, p=0.0013, Cohen's d=–1.8679) and the onset of REM sleep was delayed (t(6) = 2.043, p=0.0435, Cohen's d=0.7722, Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis of C21 effects.

claim: C21 delayed the onset of REM sleep (t(6) = 2.043, p=0.0435, Cohen's d=0.7722).
source: For REM episodes there was no C21 effect on the maximum duration, however the mean REM episode duration was increased (t(6) = 2.082, p=0.0413, Cohen's d=0.7869), the number of REM episodes reduced (t(6) = 4.942, p=0.0013, Cohen's d=–1.8679) and the onset of REM sleep was delayed (t(6) = 2.043, p=0.0435, Cohen's d=0.7722, Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis of C21 effects.

claim: C21 increased the probability to remain in the REM and NREM state.
source: State transition analysis indicated an increased probability to remain in the REM and NREM state (Figure 5d) and markers of sleep consolidation were also significantly altered as a result of C21 injections.
evidence: This is a result from state transition analysis of sleep data following C21 injection.

claim: C21 increased the amount of NREM sleep before the first occurrence of REM sleep (t(6) = 4.092, p=0.0032, Cohen's d=1.5467).
source: The amount of NREM sleep before the first occurrence of REM sleep was increased (t(6) = 4.092, p=0.0032, Cohen's d=1.5467) and brief awakenings were reduced (t(5) = 2.164, p=0.0414, Cohen's d=–0.8836; Figure 5e and f).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis of C21 effects.

claim: C21 reduced brief awakenings (t(5) = 2.164, p=0.0414, Cohen's d=–0.8836).
source: The amount of NREM sleep before the first occurrence of REM sleep was increased (t(6) = 4.092, p=0.0032, Cohen's d=1.5467) and brief awakenings were reduced (t(5) = 2.164, p=0.0414, Cohen's d=–0.8836; Figure 5e and f).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis of C21 effects.

claim: The sleep changes following CNO and C21 injections in wild-type mice bore striking similarities with those previously reported for clozapine in rats and humans.
source: The sleep changes following CNO and C21 injections in wild-type mice bore striking similarities with those previously reported for clozapine in rats (Sorge et al., 2004; Spierings et al., 1977) and humans (Hinze-Selch et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings with previously published results on clozapine.

claim: The initial suppression of REM sleep and the occurrence of longer but fewer NREM episodes were the most consistent dose-dependent effects of clozapine on sleep in male Wistar rats.
source: In particular, the initial suppression of REM sleep and the occurrence of longer but fewer NREM episodes were the most consistent dose-dependent effects of clozapine on sleep in male Wistar rats, leading the authors to conclude that clozapine has sedative effects, suppresses REM initiation and increases sleep maintenance in rats (Sorge et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study on clozapine effects in rats.

claim: In rats, low doses of clozapine (2.5 mg/kg) had immediate sleep-promoting effects while high doses (7.5 mg/kg) initially promoted wakefulness before a sustained increase in NREM sleep after the first 2 hr.
source: Interestingly, in rats low doses of clozapine (2.5 mg/kg) had immediate sleep-promoting effects while high doses of clozapine (7.5 mg/kg) initially promoted wakefulness before a sustained increase in NREM sleep after the first 2 hr (Sorge et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study on clozapine effects in rats.

claim: CNO is a competitive inhibitor of several neurotransmitter receptors, including histaminergic H1, serotoninergic 5-HT1A, 5-HT1B, 5-HT2A, 5-HT2B, muscarinic M1, M2, M3, M4, adrenergic α1A and α2A, and dopaminergic D1 and D2 receptors.
source: It has been shown that CNO is a competitive inhibitor of several neurotransmitter receptors, including histaminergic H1, serotoninergic 5-HT1A, 5-HT1B, 5-HT2A, 5-HT2B, muscarinic M1, M2, M3, M4, adrenergic α1A and α2A, and dopaminergic D1 and D2 receptors (Gomez et al., 2017; Jendryka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies characterizing CNO's off-target binding.

claim: A recent study reported increased firing rates of nigral dopaminergic neurons in wild-type rats following C21 administration.
source: In addition, a recent study reported increased firing rates of nigral dopaminergic neurons in wild-type rats, indicating that C21 can elicit direct neuromodulatory effects in rodents (Goutaudier et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study showing C21 effects on neuronal activity.

claim: C21 had a greater affinity for histamine H1 receptors than for muscarinic DREADDs.
source: Tested against a panel of G protein-coupled receptors, C21 had a greater affinity for histamine H1 receptors than for muscarinic DREADDs (Thompson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a pharmacological characterization of C21.

claim: H1 receptor knockout in mice results in a reduced number of brief awakenings, fewer but longer NREM sleep episodes, and a reduced latency to NREM sleep.
source: H1 receptor knockout and pharmacological antagonism of the H1 receptor in mice both result in a reduced number of brief awakenings, fewer but longer NREM sleep episodes, and a reduced latency to NREM sleep (Huang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on H1 receptor effects on sleep.

claim: Antihistamines strongly suppress REM sleep, but can be acutely NREM-promoting at low doses and wake-promoting at high doses.
source: In addition, antihistamines, which induce drowsiness, are known to strongly suppress REM sleep, but can be acutely NREM-promoting at low doses and wake-promoting at high doses, respectively (Ikeda-Sagara et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on antihistamine effects on sleep.

claim: The shared sleep modulatory effects of CNO and C21 might be in large part due to direct antihistaminergic action.
source: Therefore, we speculate that the shared sleep modulatory effects of CNO and C21 might be in large part due to direct antihistaminergic action.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings based on pharmacological properties.

claim: A recent study found a slight increase in NREM sleep bout duration of control mice injected with 0.3 mg/kg CNO, while all other analysed parameters were unaffected by this low CNO dose.
source: Another well-controlled study found a slight increase in NREM sleep bout duration of control mice injected with 0.3 mg/kg CNO, while all other analysed parameters were unaffected by this low CNO dose (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study showing CNO effects at low doses.

claim: NREM sleep bout duration is the sleep architectural parameter most strongly affected by CNO and C21.
source: This finding supports our effect size analysis indicating that NREM sleep bout duration is the sleep architectural parameter most strongly affected by CNO and C21 and that CNO can cause sleep-modulating effects at doses of 1 mg/kg CNO, and possibly below.
evidence: This is inferred from the effect size analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: CNO can cause sleep-modulating effects at doses of 1 mg/kg and possibly below.
source: This finding supports our effect size analysis indicating that NREM sleep bout duration is the sleep architectural parameter most strongly affected by CNO and C21 and that CNO can cause sleep-modulating effects at doses of 1 mg/kg CNO, and possibly below.
evidence: This is inferred from the effect size analysis and comparison with other studies.

claim: The hydrochloride salt preparations of CNO have reduced back-metabolism to clozapine and an improved water solubility and bioavailability compared to equivalent doses of CNO-DMSO preparations.
source: The hydrochloride salt preparations of CNO used here and in other recent sleep studies (Fernandez et al., 2018; Stucynski et al., 2021) have reduced back-metabolism to clozapine and an improved water solubility and bioavailability compared to equivalent doses of CNO-DMSO preparations (Allen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a pharmacokinetic study comparing CNO formulations.

claim: The increased bioavailability of CNO hydrochloride might explain that sleep-modulating effects are found at doses where other studies have shown no effects.
source: The increased bioavailability and thereby supposedly amplified off-target receptor binding might explain that we find sleep-modulating effects of CNO already at doses where other studies have shown no effects.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the differences between studies.

claim: This is the first study demonstrating behavioural effects of a DREADD actuator that cannot convert to clozapine.
source: While it has been described that C21 can affect neuronal firing (Goutaudier et al., 2020), to our knowledge this is the first study demonstrating behavioural effects of a DREADD actuator that cannot convert to clozapine.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings based on review of the literature.

claim: Perlapine is structurally similar to C21.
source: In line with our finding, another next-generation DREADD agonist, perlapine, which is structurally similar to C21 (Chen et al., 2015; Thompson et al., 2018), is long known as a REM-suppressing sedative and muscle relaxant used in the treatment of insomnia (Ando et al., 1970; Allen and Oswald, 1973; Stille et al., 1973).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on the chemical structure and pharmacology of perlapine and C21.

claim: Perlapine is a REM-suppressing sedative and muscle relaxant used in the treatment of insomnia.
source: In line with our finding, another next-generation DREADD agonist, perlapine, which is structurally similar to C21 (Chen et al., 2015; Thompson et al., 2018), is long known as a REM-suppressing sedative and muscle relaxant used in the treatment of insomnia (Ando et al., 1970; Allen and Oswald, 1973; Stille et al., 1973).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature on perlapine.

claim: Sleep analysis can reveal behavioural effects of DREADD agonists that are missed by other established behavioural tests such as the elevated plus maze and the marble burying task or measurements of locomotion and reaction time.
source: Our work indicates that sleep analysis can reveal behavioural effects of DREADD agonists that are missed by other established behavioural tests such as the elevated plus maze and the marble burying task or measurements of locomotion and reaction time (Jendryka et al., 2019; Tran et al., 2020).
evidence: This is inferred from the current findings showing sleep effects and citations to studies that did not detect behavioral effects with other tests.

claim: Sleep assessment could serve as a tool to evaluate the biological inertness of newly developed chemogenetic actuators.
source: Considering the complexity of neurotransmitter systems regulating sleep (Saper and Fuller, 2017) and the sensitivity of sleep architecture to pharmacological intervention (Riemann and Nissen, 2012), we propose that sleep assessment could serve as an invaluable tool to evaluate the biological inertness of newly developed chemogenetic actuators.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the findings and cited literature on sleep regulation and pharmacology.

claim: Sixteen young adult male C57BL/6J mice (age: 113±6 days, weight: 25.2±0.5 g) were used in this study.
source: Sixteen young adult male C57BL/6J mice (age: 113±6 days, weight: 25.2±0.5 g) were used in this study.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: All 16 animals were implanted with a right frontal EEG screw, a reference EEG screw above the cerebellum, and EMG wires in the neck muscles.
source: All 16 animals used in this study were implanted with a right frontal EEG screw, a reference EEG screw above the cerebellum, and EMG wires in the neck muscles as described previously (Fisher et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the surgical procedures used in the study.

claim: CNO dihydrochloride was dissolved in sterile saline.
source: To avoid the use of the toxic solvent dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), which is typically used for the preparation of CNO products in concentrations of up to 15% (Campbell and Marchant, 2018), we opted for the use of a water-soluble salt preparation of CNO, CNO dihydrochloride (Tocris, Bio-Techne LTD, Abingdon, UK, catalog no.: 6329) dissolved in sterile saline.
evidence: This is a description of the drug preparation method.

claim: All 16 animals received a medium dose of CNO (5 mg/kg) and an equivalent volume of saline in a counterbalanced order with a 72 hr rest interval between the first two experimental sessions.
source: All 16 animals received a medium dose of CNO (5 mg/kg, 0.25 mg/ml solution) and an equivalent volume of saline in a counterbalanced order with a 72 hr rest interval between the first two experimental sessions.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Of the 16 mice, 14 also received a 10 mg/kg CNO injection and 12 received a 1 mg/kg CNO injection.
source: Of those 16 mice, 14 also received a 10 mg/kg CNO injection (0.5 mg/ml solution) and 12 a 1 mg/kg CNO injection (0.05 mg/ml solution).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Seven animals received a 3 mg/kg C21 injection in a fifth experimental session.
source: Seven animals also received a 3 mg/kg (0.15 mg/ml) C21 injection in a fifth experimental session.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Intraperitoneal injections were performed within 15 min after light onset.
source: Animals were on a regular light-dark cycle (lights on at 9 am) and intraperitoneal (i.p.) injections were performed within 15 min after light onset following a brief health check.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.
